strengths: Addresses a real and under-explored gap: evaluating text-to-image models on long, detail-intensive prompts (avg. 284.89 tokens), compared to prior benchmarks limited to ~100 tokens. Table 1 makes a clear case for the benchmark's scale and coverage.

Substantial and non-trivial dataset construction: 4,116 prompts derived from human-annotated captioning datasets (DOCCI, Localized Narratives), augmented with 37,165 character attribute, 6,910 location, 12,330 scene attribute, and 18,526 relationship annotations. A mini-benchmark of 800 prompts is also provided for cheap evaluation.

The evaluation pipeline grounds MLLM judgments with auxiliary tools (YOLOE-11L open-set detector, BLIP matching, cropping/highlighting), which is a reasonable mitigation against pure-LLM self-enhancement bias, and the paper explicitly acknowledges the single-MLLM concern.

Robustness checks are unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: re-evaluation with InternVL3-9B preserving rankings, random-seed temperature=0.8 experiments showing <0.5% variation, and human evaluation of task relevance, source-image fidelity, and prompt consistency.

Comparison of 12 models (7 general-purpose + 5 long-prompt-optimized) is broad and pairs each optimized model with its appropriate backbone, allowing a cleaner attribution of gains to long-prompt training vs. context windows; the observation that gains are driven more by long-prompt training/decomposition than by larger context windows is a useful takeaway.

The negative correlation between prompt length and adherence (Fig. 3 and Appendix N) is analyzed separately for attribute alignment of present characters, distinguishing it from mere character omission; this strengthens the empirical claim.
Open-sourcing data, curation code, and evaluation tools, plus the mini-benchmark and compatibility with external metrics (aesthetics, safety), supports reproducibility and reuse.
weaknesses: The benchmark is fundamentally LLM-generated: prompts are expanded from captions via Qwen2.5-LLM/MLLM, and attributes are validated by an LLM. The 'prompt-conditional' evaluation (Section 3.1.3 and Appendix G) measures adherence to LLM-augmented descriptions rather than to naturally written human long prompts, which could bias toward the kind of compositional structure the augmentation creates. This makes the benchmark's ability to generalize to real user behavior uncertain.

Evaluation is largely MLLM-based (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) even with auxiliary grounding. The robustness appendix shows InternVL inflates all scores by 10-20 points while 'preserving rankings,' indicating that absolute accuracy figures (the headline ~50% numbers) are strongly evaluator-dependent and should not be read as calibrated.

The paper presents no new method or theoretical contribution; the causal mechanisms invoked ('encoders flatten compositional grammar', 'diffusion models suffer attribute leakage') are explicitly left as hypotheses (Section 7). The analyses in Sections 4.2.3 and 6 are descriptive and largely qualitative, with the difficulty hierarchy established primarily via the proportion-of-hard-samples heuristic.

Claims of 'first comprehensive benchmark' are strong given DPG-Bench and DensePrompts already target long prompts; the differentiator (length and attribute volume) is real but incremental, and the limitation section (Appendix O) does not engage with the risk that added attributes create artificially saturated and partly redundant prompts.

Minor inconsistencies and presentation issues: Section 4.1 refers to 'GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2025)' while tables use 'GPT Image-1'; Appendix P has garbled text/brackets; several claims in Section 6 are asserted rather than derived from new experiments.

Evaluation treats 'Scene Attributes' accuracy above 90% while Character Locations ~40-50% as evidence of a metric hierarchy, but this may partly reflect differing granularity/triviality of the underlying questions rather than genuinely separable competence; the paper does not control for annotation difficulty across categories.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically important gap: evaluating text-to-image models on long, detail-intensive prompts, whereas most existing benchmarks focus on short captions.

It provides a large benchmark (4,116 prompts, average 284.89 tokens) with annotations across four useful dimensions: character attributes, character locations, scene attributes, and entity relationships.
The data construction pipeline is described in substantial detail, including grounding via auxiliary tools (YOLOE, BLIP) and human validation of benchmark data quality.

The paper evaluates 12 models, including general-purpose and long-prompt-optimized systems, and provides extensive appendices with robustness checks, mini-benchmark results, randomness analysis, and limitations.
The analysis attempts to go beyond aggregate scores by studying the relationship between prompt length and adherence, difficulty hierarchy, and failure patterns.
The claimed release of dataset, curation code, evaluation tools, and a mini-benchmark would be a useful community resource if properly provided and maintained.
weaknesses: The central evaluation protocol is not validated against human judgments of generated images. All four metrics rely on a single MLLM evaluator (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) making yes/no decisions, while the human study only validates the benchmark annotations, not whether the metric scores reflect human assessment of model outputs. This is a critical evidential gap for the headline claims.

The absolute model scores are strongly evaluator-dependent. Re-evaluating with InternVL3-9B inflates scores dramatically (e.g., DeepFloyd IF object 31.0 to 54.8, FLUX.1-dev object 51.5 to 71.4, GPT Image-1 entity relationships 63.1 to 82.5). The paper calls Qwen 'stricter' but provides no human ground truth to establish which evaluator is correct, so claims such as 'SOTA models achieve merely ~50%' are not well supported.

The metrics are recall-oriented and do not meaningfully penalize extraneous content, hallucinations, or extra objects/attributes. A model can satisfy specified attributes while adding many unmentioned details. The scene-attribute metric is especially coarse, often reducing to broad checks such as 'realistic photo' or 'daytime', which many images satisfy regardless of prompt understanding.

The long prompts are generated by LLM augmentation and are often repetitive and redundant. The appendix examples repeat the same entities and attributes multiple times (e.g., repeated mentions of 'white mug with whipped cream' and 'cookies'), so the 285-token average may reflect verbosity rather than informative detail. This raises construct-validity concerns: the benchmark may measure robustness to repetitive text rather than compositional long-prompt understanding.

Comparisons with proprietary models are not controlled for internal prompt rewriting. GPT Image-1 and Gemini are accessed via APIs with default hyperparameters and may internally rewrite or expand prompts, confounding prompt-adherence measurement. Output resolutions also differ (512 for SD1.5-family models vs 1024 for others), which may affect MLLM judgments of detail.

The paper does not demonstrate that DetailMaster reveals failures beyond existing long-prompt benchmarks such as DPG-Bench or DensePrompts. There is no cross-benchmark correlation, no comparison of model rankings, and no human-preference or human-adherence validation of the new metrics. The claim of being the 'first comprehensive benchmark' is therefore overstated.

The human evaluation is limited and partly circular. It samples 50 examples per task, averages two annotators, reports no inter-annotator agreement, and finds 100% task relevance—which is expected because the tasks are defined by the annotations. It does not validate the automatic evaluation of generated images.

Potential data contamination is unaddressed. The prompts are derived from COCO, Flickr30k, and DOCCI images likely present in T2I training data, with no decontamination or overlap analysis. Absolute performance may be inflated by memorization or familiarity with those images.

Metric details introduce noise: the main Character Attributes metric conflates character omission with attribute misalignment; location regions overlap (e.g., 'upper' and 'middle'), making 'precise' positional judgments ambiguous; and character detection relies on a dual-model pipeline whose detection errors are not reported.

The data construction filters for samples with more than four main characters and at least four valid character-level attributes, biasing the benchmark toward crowded, multi-object scenes rather than general long-prompt scenarios. This limits diversity and practical representativeness.

The prompt-length analysis confounds length with content complexity. Longer prompts likely contain more attributes, objects, and relationships, so the negative correlation between length and accuracy may reflect task difficulty rather than context length per se. No controls or significance tests are provided.

Presentation and reproducibility need improvement. There is no visible anonymized link to the dataset/code; the pipeline depends on proprietary APIs and specific model versions; table headers inconsistently use 'Entity Relationships', 'Spatial/Interactive Relationships', and 'Spatial Attributes'; the reference list contains duplicates and errors; and some central mechanistic claims (e.g., text encoders 'flatten' grammar) are asserted as hypotheses without causal validation.

strengths: Introduces a much-needed benchmark for long, detail-rich text-to-image prompts: 4,116 prompts averaging 284.89 tokens, with four fine-grained evaluation dimensions (character attributes, structured locations, scene attributes, and entity relationships), substantially extending prior long-prompt benchmarks that typically stay around 100 tokens.

The data construction pipeline is carefully engineered, using human-annotated detailed captions plus auxiliary visual grounding (open-set detection, cropping/highlighting, MLLM-based extraction, filtering). Human evaluation supports high dataset quality, with 100% task relevance, 93.6% source-image fidelity, and 97.5% prompt consistency.

The experimental study is extensive: 12 models are evaluated, including seven general-purpose and five long-prompt-optimized systems. The results reveal useful insights, e.g., that long-prompt training and decomposition can matter more than simply enlarging context windows, and that performance degrades consistently as prompt length increases.

Robustness checks strengthen the benchmark: rankings and major conclusions are largely preserved with an alternative MLLM evaluator (InternVL3-9B), random seeds produce negligible variance, and a Mini-Benchmark is provided for resource-constrained evaluation.

The authors release dataset, data-curation code, and evaluation tools, and provide detailed implementation/config information, resource-consumption analysis, and an honest limitations section. This substantially supports reproducibility and future use.

The paper addresses an important practical gap: professional and interactive T2I applications increasingly require long, compositional prompts, and existing benchmarks offer limited diagnostics for such settings.
weaknesses: The automatic evaluation relies heavily on a single MLLM family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), while human validation covers data annotation quality rather than agreement between the automatic metric and human judgments on generated images. The alternative-evaluator experiment preserves rankings but inflates scores significantly, so absolute numbers (e.g., '~50% accuracy') are evaluator-dependent and should not be treated as definitive.

The benchmark is constructed through LLM/MLLM augmentation, and human evaluation reveals non-trivial hallucination rates for some visual alignments (e.g., 88.58% entity-relationship alignment, 91.58% person-attribute alignment). This weakens claims that all prompt details are faithfully grounded in source images, even if the benchmark primarily measures prompt-following rather than source reconstruction.

The main 'Character Attributes' metric appears to conflate character omission with attribute misbinding. Table 3 shows much higher attribute accuracy when only detected characters are considered, which suggests the headline attribute failure rates may partly reflect detection/omission failures rather than pure attribute leakage. This distinction should be more clearly disentangled in the main metric.

The mechanistic explanations ('encoders flatten compositional grammar,' 'diffusion models suffer attribute leakage') are not directly tested and remain hypotheses. The abstract's wording implies stronger causal evidence than the paper provides; the conclusion appropriately softens this, but the main claims should be more carefully scoped.

The negative correlation between prompt length and accuracy is observational. Prompt length is likely confounded with prompt difficulty, source dataset, number of entities, and scene complexity. A controlled length-perturbation study would better support the causal interpretation.

Potential data contamination or overlap with model training data is not discussed, despite prompts being derived from public datasets such as DOCCI and Localized Narratives. This could affect evaluation fairness and should at least be acknowledged or analyzed.

There are minor presentation/terminology inconsistencies (e.g., 'Entity Relationships' vs. 'Spatial Attributes' in tables, occasional typos/model-name inconsistencies). These do not undermine the paper but should be fixed for clarity and reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses a clear gap in Text-to-Image evaluation: long, detail-rich prompts with fine-grained compositional constraints, which are increasingly relevant for professional applications.

Comprehensive benchmark: 4,116 prompts averaging 284.89 tokens, covering four well-motivated dimensions (Character Attributes, Character Locations, Scene Attributes, Spatial/Interactive Relationships) with large annotation counts (e.g., 37,165 character attributes, 18,526 relationships).

Automated data construction pipeline grounded in real image-caption pairs (DOCCI, Localized Narratives) with auxiliary tools (open-set detector, BLIP) and human validation, achieving high reported fidelity (93.6% visual alignment, 97.5% prompt consistency).

Extensive evaluation of 19 models across five paradigms, revealing consistent negative correlation between prompt length and adherence, and a clear difficulty hierarchy (Character Locations hardest, Scene Attributes easiest).

Controlled ablation study with a modified SD-XL that disentangles token limit from training prompt length, showing long-prompt training matters more than merely expanding context windows—a valuable insight for the community.

Strong reproducibility: detailed configurations, inference hyperparameters, LLM prompts, and robustness checks across different evaluator MLLMs, random seeds, and smaller evaluators; open-source commitment for data and code.
Resource-efficient variants (mini benchmark, lightweight 3B evaluator) that preserve model rankings, facilitating broader adoption under computational constraints.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on LLM/MLLM for both prompt construction and evaluation; despite auxiliary tools and cross-evaluator checks, inherent biases and potential hallucinations in the generated prompts/annotations may not be fully eliminated.
Human evaluation is limited to 400 samples (50 per task), which provides only a spot-check of data quality and may not generalize to the full 4,116-prompt benchmark.

The ablation study uses a single modified SD-XL architecture with a specific connector and training data; conclusions about the relative importance of token limit versus long-prompt training may not generalize to other backbones or training regimes.

Prompts are augmented with LLM-extracted details that may not be present in the original source images; while evaluation is prompt-conditional, this could reduce ecological validity and introduce unnatural or physically inconsistent combinations.
No dedicated limitations section; potential negative societal impacts (e.g., misuse for generating harmful content) are only briefly mentioned in the impact statement.
Model comparisons lack statistical significance testing or confidence intervals, making it difficult to assess whether observed differences between models are meaningful beyond point estimates.

strengths: Constructs a genuinely long-prompt benchmark: 4,116 prompts averaging 284.89 tokens with structured annotations, clearly exceeding prior long-prompt/compositional benchmarks (DensePrompts ≈100 tokens, DPG-Bench ≈84 tokens; Table 1), and covering four well-motivated compositional dimensions.

Broad, useful empirical study spanning 19 models across five paradigms (Table 2), plus a controlled 2×2 ablation (Table 3) that cleanly separates expanded context (77 vs 512 tokens) from long-prompt training, supporting the plausible and useful conclusion that training data matters more than raw context length.

Above-average reproducibility and robustness tooling: open-sourced data/code, a 800-prompt mini-benchmark, a 3B lightweight evaluator, cross-evaluator (Qwen2.5-VL vs InternVL3) and random-seed analyses, and compatibility with external quality/safety metrics (Appendix J, K, L, M, N).

The data-construction pipeline meaningfully grounds LLM outputs using an open-set detector (YOLOE), BLIP matching, image cropping/highlighting, and few-shot prompting (Appendices B, H, V), reducing the risk of a purely end-to-end LLM-generated dataset; human evaluation reports 100% task relevance and ~97.5% prompt consistency.

The controlled ablation is complemented by a short-prompt check on T2I-CompBench (Table 21) showing the long-prompt-trained models do not regress on short prompts, which strengthens the generalization argument.
weaknesses: The central evaluation rests entirely on a single 7B MLLM judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), and the paper validates the *data quality* but never validates the *evaluator's judgments on generated images* against human ground truth. Since the headline claims (e.g., 'Character Locations is the hardest dimension,' a ~50% ceiling for SOTA) are derived from these judgments, the core contribution—a 'rigorous' and 'robust' evaluation workflow—is asserted more than demonstrated.

Cross-evaluator results expose very large absolute discrepancies that the paper reports only as rank correlation. For example, SD-XL Object score moves 24.41 (QwenVL, Table 2) → 36.41 (InternVL, Table 10), and DeepFloyd IF 31.01 → 54.75 (a ~75% relative swing). With no ground-truth calibration, it is unclear which numbers are correct, so absolute metric values and the derived 'difficulty hierarchy' are unreliable; a benchmark's utility depends on its absolute numbers being meaningful, not just its rankings.

The 'grounded in real image-caption pairs … visual realism' selling point is partially undermined by LLM-based prompt expansion. Human evaluation itself reports that 8–11% of annotations do not align with the source image (Person attributes 91.58%, light 91%, Entity Relationships 88.58%; Tables 5–8). The defense that evaluation is prompt-conditional is reasonable, but it means a non-trivial fraction of evaluated constraints may be fabricated by the LLM and a model is penalized for not following potentially arbitrary/hallucinated details.

Novelty is incremental. Conceptually the benchmark is close to existing compositional/long-prompt benchmarks (DPG-Bench, DensePrompts, GenAI-Bench, T2I-CompBench), differing mainly in prompt length and the number of constraints, while reusing a standard MLLM-VQA scoring paradigm. The 'new understanding' (encoder failures, attribute leakage) is plausible but not deeply mechanistically investigated—the Discussion explicitly defers the mechanism to future work.

The headline metrics conflate character omission with attribute-binding failure (attributes of ungenerated characters are scored wrong). The paper acknowledges this and offers an auxiliary 'accuracy over present characters' analysis (Appendix S), but this is not integrated into the primary metric, so the main numbers may understate models' true binding ability and make the benchmark look harder than it is.

Discriminative utility is questionable given the score floor: Character Locations ranges 8–54% and Entity Relationships 6–63% across all 19 models, and Scene Attributes saturates near 95–99% for advanced models. When one dimension is near-floor and another near-ceiling, the benchmark compresses model differences in precisely the dimensions it claims to diagnose. Additionally, several results depend on non-deterministic, version-pinned proprietary APIs (GPT Image-1, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Nano Banana 2), which are not reproducible, and some cited works/evaluations are tied to future or unpinned 2026 model versions.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: faithful text-to-image generation from long, detail-rich prompts with complex compositional constraints.

Introduces a substantial benchmark with 4,116 prompts averaging 284.89 tokens, covering four fine-grained dimensions: Character Attributes, Character Locations, Scene Attributes, and Spatial/Interactive Relationships.
The data construction pipeline is carefully designed, combining human-annotated captioning datasets, MLLM-based extraction, open-set detection, and multiple validation/filtering steps.
Human validation supports high data quality: 100% task relevance, 93.6% source-image fidelity, and 97.5% prompt consistency, with detailed per-task results in the appendix.

Extensive evaluation across 19 models and five paradigms, including classical diffusion, long-prompt-optimized models, LLM/MLLM-encoder models, autoregressive/unified models, and proprietary SOTA models.

Robustness checks are strong for a benchmark paper: cross-evaluator validation with InternVL3, small-evaluator feasibility with Qwen2.5-VL-3B, random-seed analysis, and Kendall's Tau correlations across evaluators.
The controlled ablation disentangles token limit and long-prompt training, providing useful evidence that capacity alone is insufficient.
Reproducibility is well supported: open-source data/code, detailed inference configurations, construction prompts, resource/time usage, mini-benchmark, and lightweight evaluator options.

The paper yields actionable insights, including a clear difficulty hierarchy, negative correlation between prompt length and adherence, and evidence of attribute leakage under detail-heavy conditions.
weaknesses: The automated LLM/MLLM construction pipeline may still introduce hallucinated or weakly grounded attributes. Human evaluation shows ~91.6% person-attribute alignment and ~88.6% relationship-image alignment, meaning some annotations are not perfectly faithful to source images.

Because evaluation is prompt-conditional rather than source-image-conditional, this is defensible, but the benchmark may contain prompts that are not fully realistic or logically consistent with the original scene.

The primary evaluation relies on a single MLLM judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct). Robustness checks show that absolute scores vary substantially with evaluator choice (e.g., InternVL3 tends to inflate scores), and no human evaluation of generated images is reported, so metric validity remains partially unverified.

The main causal claim that long-prompt training matters more than expanded context length is supported only by one modified SD-XL architecture and one training setup; generalization to other architectures and training regimes is not established.
The human evaluation sample is relatively modest (400 annotations total) and lacks inter-annotator agreement statistics, which limits confidence in annotation reliability.

Some design choices in the ablation study, especially how '77-token limit with long-prompt training' is implemented, are not fully clear from the main text and could affect interpretation of the claimed synergy.

The benchmark's long prompts are constructed through iterative LLM expansion; without stronger manual spot-checking or external validation, there is some risk of systematic stylistic or semantic artifacts that favor or penalize particular model families.
